To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
UV-irradiation of the skin of a mouse induces long-lasting alterations to dendritic cell progenitors in the mouse bone marrow.
erythemal UV irradiation induces a long-term alteration in dendritic cells that are derived from bone marrow and reside in the periphery of mice.
UV-irradiation of the skin of C57BL/6 mice alters the function of BM-derived DCs for at least 16 weeks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of ultraviolet (UV) radiation on the immune system and the skin, and in particular, on the role of dendritic cells (DCs) in UV-induced immune suppression and carcinogenesis.
the long-term immunosuppression that occurs in mice following exposure of the mouse skin to erythemal UVR.
the long-term effects of exposure to UV radiation (U VR).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the UV-induced alterations in DCs in the periphery are not due to the UV-induced alterations of the hematopoietics cells in the BM, but are due to an epigenetic alteration of the DC progenitors in BM.
UVR-induced epigenetic changes in BM progenitor cells result in long-lasting changes to the immune function and DC activity in the periphery of mice.
UVR-induced alterations to DC progenitors in BM may contribute to long lasting systemic immunosuppresion (>28d) after exposure to erythemal doses of UVR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the UV-induced epigenetic changes are long-lasting and affect the function of dendritic cells in the skin and the draining lymph nodes.
UV radiation can alter the function of the dendritic cells that arise from the bone marrow.
the immune system is altered by UV exposure, which may be due to epigenetic changes to hematopoietic stem cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the UV radiation-induced epigenetic changes that we observed in the bone marrow are long lasting and are passed on to the next generation of cells.
UV radiation (UVA or UVB) exposure can alter the immune system in a way that can be transmitted to the offspring of the irradiated animal.
UV irradiation of the skin of a mouse has an effect on its bone marrow.
